name: Numbered perfumery / analogs

lead: Numbered perfumery refers to fragrance houses and lines that label products with numbers or codes instead of evocative names, often so that each code corresponds to a known scent it is modeled on. These analogs, also called dupes, clones or inspired-by fragrances, let a person smell like a popular designer or niche perfume without paying its price. Scent is part of grooming and first impressions, so the payoff is smelling the way an expensive fragrance is meant to smell.

Independent write-ups describe three categories: clones that aim to replicate one fragrance, inspired-by scents that borrow its character, and similar scents that share notes. They report that almost none are identical to the target, with differences in the opening, longevity and complexity.

paras: People pick a fragrance they like from a designer or niche house, find an analog that reviewers describe as matching it, and wear it as they would any perfume. Some buy small sizes first. Prices in retail guides run roughly $15 to $60 for analogs against roughly $200 to $400 for the originals.

Perfume ingredients can irritate or trigger allergies in some people. Reviewers say analogs often last fewer hours on skin than the originals and may smell flatter as they dry down. Sellers of counterfeit bottles of the original brands are a separate issue from honestly labeled analogs.

web.title: Fragrance Dupes: Which Ones Are Worth It, and Which Are Oversold

chain: Pick a scent associated with a popular fragrance
Smell like a well-regarded fragrance at lower cost
angle.text: The analog delivers a similar scent directly on skin. Reviewers say it can come close but generally differs in opening, longevity and development.

lead: Numbered perfumery / analogs describes a style of fragrance retail in which products are identified by numbers or codes and are designed to reproduce the scent of a well-known perfume. They belong to the wider category of fragrance dupes, which a 2020s buyer's guide divides into clones that aim to copy a specific fragrance, inspired-by scents that take its general character and add a twist, and similar scents that share notes by chance.[1]

For appearance purposes, the use is grooming: fragrance is part of how a person presents and is perceived, and analogs let people wear a recognizable, popular scent at lower cost. The same guide reports that luxury originals cost around $200 to $400 while dupes are around $20 to $50.[1]

Commercial perfume formulas are treated as trade secrets rather than patented, and analog makers use similar aromatic compounds in their own formulations.[1][2] Differences from the original show up mainly in the opening, longevity and complexity.[1]
infobox: Numbers or codes instead of names
Described as legal original formulations; counterfeit bottles are a separate matter [1]
Eau de parfum about 15-20%, extrait about 15-30% [2]

paras: A buyer's guide on Fragplace says clone fragrances aim to replicate a specific perfume, inspired-by fragrances capture the general character with their own twist, and similar scents share a vibe or notes. It says almost none smell identical and that differences typically appear in the first 15 to 30 minutes, where cheaper versions often use synthetics, and in longevity and complexity.[1]

Named examples in that guide include alternatives to Baccarat Rouge 540, Santal 33 and Creed-type fragrances such as Club de Nuit Intense Man, described as an alternative to Aventus.[1] Wikipedia's perfume article notes that synthetic materials have long been used to copy natural scents and that concentrations vary between houses.[2]

The guide reports that dupes often last less time than originals, giving the example of 8 or more hours for a luxury fragrance against 4 to 6 for a dupe, while some budget options are praised for projection. It says formulas are not patented the way brand names are, so dupes are legal original formulations, and that its warning concerns counterfeit bottles of originals rather than honestly labeled dupes.[1]
